title: Selling to friends
content:
There are two versions, very different:

FAVOR: This is what multi-level marketing preys on. You ask a family member or a friend to buy something, not because they need it, but because you do.

This doesn’t always end well. Someone might want to further their relationship with you by doing you this favor, but if the unspoken promise is that the item or service is worthwhile, the disappointment that ensues hurts everyone. Real estate brokers or middlemen in a bind often seek to build friendly relationships at the club or community meetings, but then try to leverage this friendship into a significant sale without doing the hard work of actually being the best choice.

TRUST: This is the sort of sale that happens when you begin with the benefit of the doubt but actually deliver a great outcome. You’ll know this is the case when the person who trusted you ends up testifying on your behalf to others.

“No pressure” is something that’s showing up more and more in the pitches I’m seeing. Of course, there’s no pressure! Just saying it implies that you wish there were.

If you’re asking for a favor, you’re not serving and you’re not selling. You’re trading.

And if you’re asking for trust, be prepared to honor the obligation it creates.

title: The Man Who Saw Cats in Human Faces
content:
Imagine feline forms haunting every human face you encounter as you go about your day. Seeing these Cheshire cats flickering into view, you might think you had tumbled down the rabbit hole. It seems phantasmagorical. But this is the experience of a 28-year-old man named Karl who lives in the northeastern United States.

When Karl wakes in the morning, his gray tabby Luna is often the first being he greets, and Luna’s face, the first he gazes upon: the whiskers, the almond eyes, the pink nose, the stripes. When this happens, the image of Luna’s face sticks with him for several hours or even the rest of his day. He sees his feline companion’s eyes and silver stripes superimposed over all of the human faces that he glimpses, both in person and online.

**Read more:**[**“How Does Your Brain Know A Cat Is A Cat?”**](https://nautil.us/how-does-your-brain-know-a-cat-is-a-cat-1280394)

The reverse is also true: If the first face he sees in the morning is a human one, he will see that person’s pupils and eye shape superimposed on every other face he sees that day, including the furry mug of his pet cat. These superpositions are seamless: The faces otherwise appear normal and coherent.

Karl’s visions began after he had brain surgery to remove some abnormally connected blood vessels from his right posterior temporal lobe, the command center for recognizing a person’s identity and reading their facial expressions. These visions, and more run-of-the-mill face distortions, where faces simply don't look right, have plagued Karl for two years post-surgery. He appears to have developed a combination of two rare neurological conditions: palinopsia, where an image persists in someone’s field of vision after exposure, and prosopometamorphopsia, where a person sees distorted faces.

Brad Duchaine, a professor and psychologist at Dartmouth University, heard about Karl through Jennifer Nosker, a neuropsychologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital who worked with Karl after his surgery. When Karl told Nosker about his face distortions, she found Duchaine’s work on the subject, and contacted him. At Dartmouth’s Social Perception Lab, Duchaine has been studying prosopometamorphopsia for many years, collecting accounts through a website dedicated to the condition. Over the past five years, around 275 individuals have contacted the lab through the [site](https://prosopometamorphopsia.faceblind.org/).

“Karl finds the transfers between cat and human faces very strange,” writes Duchaine, in an email. “He has had problems with face perception for some time, though, so he has adapted to them and takes them in stride.” All of his distortions began after his surgery, Duchaine explains.

Duchaine and Nosker recently [published](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0010945226002649?via%3Dihub) a case study about Karl in the journal _Cortex_ together with a third colleague, Antonio Mello, a psychologist at Dartmouth.

Ordinarily, people with prosopometamorphopsia see alterations in the shape or position of facial features or in the color or texture of skin. For example, some people with the condition [see](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(24)00136-3/abstract) eyes and mouths stretched into “demonic” shapes, with grooves in the forehead, or they might [see](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36813107/) features drooping, swelling or twisting. Face substitutions are an atypical expression of this unusual condition.

Poodle Party: According to a report from 1986, following a stroke, patient 2 transposed the face of a poodle she saw onto every face she saw for at least 30 minutes. _Credit: AI-generated images generated by Brad Duchaine_

One of the earliest documented cases of face substitution in the scientific literature also involved a pet: a poodle. According to a [case study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S001094528680048X?via%3Dihub) published in _Cortex_ in 1986, a woman known as “patient 2” was riding a bus about 9 months after a stroke when she saw a poodle in the lap of another passenger. After she looked away from the dog, however, she noticed everyone else in the bus seemed to suddenly have the poodle’s face in place of their human one. This visual hallucination continued for another 30 minutes, even after she got off the bus.

At the time, the implications of her experience seemed quite shocking: Her visions suggested that the brain processes faces differently from other categories of visual stimuli, an idea that is now widely accepted. Studies have [found](https://www.science.org/content/article/identifying-brains-own-facial-recognition-system?referrer=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.google.com%2F) that the fusiform gyrus, a region of the temporal lobe, becomes active when a person is looking at faces, and only faces.

The cases of Karl and patient 2 differ in at least two ways, wrote Duchaine. “First, the woman in the 1986 case saw the poodle’s whole face on the bus passengers, but Karl sees only parts carried over, mainly the eyes and pupils. Second, the 1986 transfer went one way, from dog to human. Karl’s goes both ways. If he sees his cat first, its eyes appear on people. If he sees a person first, that person’s eyes can appear on his cat.”

In their recent analysis, Duchaine and his colleagues used artificial intelligence to generate photorealistic versions of the visions that both Karl and patient 2 might have experienced. Karl helped to revise the cat-human hybrids to match his experience, while the poodle heads were generated using line drawings made in 1986.

The images are reminiscent of the works of [Matthew Grabelsky](https://www.grabelsky.com/), a contemporary American artist who creates hyperrealistic oil paintings of humans with animal heads riding the New York City subway, and surrealist painter and novelist [Leonora Carrington](https://www.moma.org/artists/993-leonora-carrington), who incorporated horse-headed women and other human-animal hybrids into her works.

Karl and patient 2 remind us that our perception of faces crosses species lines. If a single region of the brain is fundamentally wired to recognize faces in both people as well as cats and dogs, this ability may share a common anatomical blueprint that dates back hundreds of millions of years. It might even help explain why we are so quick to attribute human emotions and personalities to the other creatures with whom we share the planet and our homes. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Sniffing Out the Link Between Odor and Disease
content:
_[This story](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/health-disease/2026/disease-sniffing-tests-get-closer-to-reality) was originally published by_[Knowable Magazine](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/society/2026/prehistory-lost-threads)_._

When social anthropologist Hanna Marie Ihlebæk interviewed nurses at a Norwegian cancer ward for her PhD thesis, she was surprised to learn that many of them relied on their sense of smell in their work. “Urine infection is really distinct, I can recognize that smell in the corridor!” one of the nurses said. Another claimed to be able to pick out digestive bleeding and cell necrosis. “I don’t know what I would have done without my ability to smell,” said a third.

Long ago, in the 5th century BCE, the Greek physician-philosopher Hippocrates held that disease could be identified by body odor. In modern times, we have stories of [Oscar the cat](https://www.nejm.org/doi/abs/10.1056/NEJMp078108) who seemed to perceive which residents would soon pass away at a Rhode Island nursing home, and dogs that have been used to detect bladder cancer, malaria and Covid-19. In Africa, [giant pouched rats](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-01751-9) are employed to sniff out tuberculosis.

For years, scientists have been exploring how the molecules that waft from our breath or skin might be harnessed to sniff out a laundry list of diseases — Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s, certain cancers, the flu and the common cold. Yet the field has struggled to bring such tests to the clinic. Now, with new tools that can detect tiny amounts of molecules, as well as [advances in machine learning](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/acssensors.4c02843), that goal appears within reach. A variety of ailments might soon be efficiently diagnosed with non-invasive tests that employ devices as simple as Breathalyzers.

“It’s really, really exciting,” says Mark Woollam, a chemical biologist at the University of Indianapolis.

**Telltale Molecules**

A handful of [breath-based tests are already in use](http://arjournals.annualreviews.org/eprint/CzsMqAbWqpaztkfZzYtY/full/10.1146/annurev-anchem-071213-020043), such as one that detects gastric infection by _Helicobacter pylori_, a major cause of stomach ulcers. Patients drink a solution spiked with urea containing a “heavy” version of carbon; if _H. pylori_ is present, the bacterium will use the urea to make carbon dioxide and the test will detect that heavy-carbon CO 2 in the patients’ breath. But tests like that require swallowing a special substance and shipping a sample to a lab for analysis. Today, researchers are also working to develop tests that could give results directly at home, or at a doctor’s office. They are designed to sniff out volatile organic compounds, or VOCs. Such compounds are mostly in gas form at room temperature and can be emitted from breath, sweat, urine, blood and fecal matter.

To collect breath for analysis, for example, volunteers breathe into small, lab-grade plastic bags that resemble juice pouches, or into syringe-like breath samplers. Such samples are then analyzed in a lab with a technique called gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Other tests employ cheaper and more portable electronic noses, which are made of a series of sensors that can pick out various molecules.

Breath samples may be collected using lightweight plastic devices (top) or modified plastic pouches outfitted with valves (bottom). _CREDITS: Markes International LTD. (top); A. Vicent-Claramunt & E. Naujalis / Methodsx 2021 (bottom)_

Figuring out what molecules are significant and what conclusions can be drawn from an individual sample makes the development of such tests “very, very challenging,” Woollam says. Breath can contain contaminants from the surrounding air (think pollution or cigarette smoke), and the composition of breath can vary from one moment to another, making it hard to standardize tests and interpret single measurements. “From sitting to lying, you change your breath profile. You hold your breath, you change your breath profile. You take a drug, you change your breath profile… So how do you want to sort that out?” says chemist [Wolfram Miekisch](https://anaesthesie.med.uni-rostock.de/forschung/atemgasanalytik-ag-rombat/team), of the University Medical Center Rostock in Germany.

But researchers have made progress in pinpointing [molecules that are markers](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/health-disease/2023/saliva-next-frontier-cancer-detection) of specific diseases. When tumors grow, for example, oxidative stress in the body increases, which leads to the breakdown of fatty molecules within cells into smaller, volatile compounds, Woollam says. One study that tested the breath of [patients before and after a surgery to remove lung tumors](https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S2589537022001146) identified 16 such compounds that might serve as lung cancer breath biomarkers, including pentanal, foul-smelling butyric acid, woody hexanal and decanal, which smells like orange peel. In other research, analyses of molecules emitted from melanoma biopsy samples suggested that compounds such as the pungent chemical called [4-methyl decane](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0013813)could serve as a biomarker.

Molecules in urine could also offer clues to cancer. Woollam and colleagues analyzed [molecules wafting from the urine](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6694/15/4/1352) of men undergoing a prostate cancer biopsy and found that a panel of six molecules could detect the disease in 75 percent of cases. While it’s less sensitive than the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood-based test, the VOC method gave fewer false positives, which could help patients avoid unnecessary treatment.

Some cancer tests based on volatile compounds emanating from urine may soon hit the market. One such test by the biotech company TOBY, named after the trail-sniffing dog in Sherlock Holmes books, is designed to detect bladder cancer. Rather than looking for a single biomarker, TOBY’s test uses AI to analyze patterns of molecules wafting from urine. It was granted Breakthrough Device designation (which can speed up approval) by the US Food and Drug Administration in 2026, validating its potential; its developers say it is about a year away from commercial launch. The TOBY team is also working on a similar test for Alzheimer’s, which received the FDA’s Breakthrough Device designation in May.

**The Smell of Parkinson’s**

Clues to disease also reside in sebum, an oily, sticky substance produced by tiny glands in hair follicles. Researchers are investigating the link between volatiles emanating from sebum and Parkinson’s disease, which tends to be diagnosed late, meaning patients go longer without their symptoms being properly managed.

Hints of the sebum signal emerged many years ago: A woman named [Joy Milne](https://scienceofparkinsons.com/2021/03/12/joy/#more-63725) noticed that her husband’s body odor had turned unpleasantly woody and musky. Fourteen years later, Les Milne was diagnosed with early-onset Parkinson’s disease, and at a Parkinson’s awareness lecture, Joy noticed that the other Parkinson’s patients seemed to have a similar odor. She connected with scientists at the University of Edinburgh, and then with Parkinson’s researcher Perdita Barran. Barran and her team ran an experiment and found that Joy’s [nose could distinguish](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/mind/2024/peter-mombaerts-how-sense-of-smell-works-identify-odors) T-shirts worn by Parkinson’s patients from those worn by healthy people.

Since then, Milne and Barran, at the University of Manchester, have worked together to identify a Parkinson’s signal in the sebum molecules. “If I swabbed your back, I would find about 20,000 compounds. And if you had Parkinson’s, about 2,000 of them — so, 10 percent — would be different to people who don’t have Parkinson’s,” Barran says. These compounds include [acyl-carnitines — molecules that shuttle fatty acids into mitochondria](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-21669-4) for energy production — and others linked to perturbations in fatty acid metabolism.

Joy Milne noticed that her husband and other people with Parkinson’s emitted a specific scent. Milne is now part of a research team at the University of Manchester that’s developing a related test for diagnosing the disease. _Credit: The University of Manchester_

The sebum signature can correctly [identify over 84 percent](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acscentsci.0c01028) of people with Parkinson’s when the disease is well underway. But the test also may help spot Parkinson’s early on, before clear-cut symptoms appear. In a 2025 report, Barran and her colleagues, including Milne, studied the sebum of people who have REM sleep behavior disorder, in which they physically act out their dreams — kicking their spouse in bed while dreaming of playing soccer, for example. This condition has been strongly linked to the later development of neurodegenerative conditions. Sebum VOC profiles in this group were somewhere in between [those with diagnosed Parkinson’s disease and healthy volunteers](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-025-01026-8), the researchers reported.

**Virus or Bacteria?**

And other tests may be on the horizon. Researchers are probing potential breath signatures for the flu, for example; one 2022 study, examining 235 patients, found that some breath biomarkers [could distinguish the flu from similar infection](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36267247/)s with 78 percent accuracy. Exhaled breath might also be used to diagnose infections with the common cold: Another team found that concentrations of compounds such as [waxy-smelling](https://scent.vn/en/pages/compound/38-dimethylundecane-86540) 3,8-dimethyl-undecane in breath [correlate with rhinovirus viral loads](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8663017/) in the nose and throat.

“What the virus does, it goes to a cell, enters the cell, replicates itself, and then blasts the cell,” Miekisch says. Parts of the destroyed cell may then be emitted in a sick person’s breath, he explains, while other biomarkers come from the changes within our own metabolism in response to the infection.

Still other researchers are looking for ways to discern viral infections from bacterial ones. Bacteria [emit their own VOCs](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/374762410_Volatilomes_of_human_infection), which can be picked up in human breath (_Helicobacter pylori_, the bacterium behind [stomach ulcers](https://myhealth.alberta.ca/Health/pages/conditions.aspx?hwid=abh0960), [smells sulfurous](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s00216-023-04986-z.pdf), for example). Ilaria Belluomo, a medical biotechnologist at [Imperial College London](https://profiles.imperial.ac.uk/i.belluomo), and her colleagues are running a study on bacterial and viral signatures in the breath of children hospitalized for severe lung infections. “A test that can discriminate the two types of infections can be completely transformative,” she says. By revealing whether an infection is bacterial, it would help discern whether taking antibiotics makes sense, potentially reducing antibiotic overuse, Belluomo says.

One of the most promising applications of research on volatile biomarkers of infection would be in the ICU, Miekisch says. It could make it possible to continuously monitor the breath of intubated, critically ill patients to spot early signs of danger. For example, distinguishing between sepsis, which is caused by bacteria, and the autoimmune reaction called systemic inflammatory response syndrome is “an important question,” he says.

Yet obstacles remain. One is a lack of standardization, so it is difficult to compare results between different studies. Another hurdle is not having a good grasp on where these biomarkers are coming from, Miekisch says. And some tests that looked promising went on to fail in larger studies or lacked the funding to get to market.

But many VOC scientists remain optimistic. “Although VOC research has faced numerous challenges, the field continues to make remarkable progress,” Woollam says. Perhaps patients won’t have to hold their breath for too long, after all. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Scientists Just Found Something Strange Under the Skin of Sea Pigs
content:
The translucent blobs of flesh that are sea pigs are some of the most unusual sights in the deep ocean. They’re also difficult to study. Some of them live more than 32,800 feet below the surface, so getting eyes on them isn’t easy.

Now researchers have made a new discovery about the microbes that call these sea pigs home. Having symbiotic bacteria living under the skin isn’t unusual for these types of creatures, but a recent study [published](https://doi.org/10.1093/ismehm/aazag018) in _ISME Host Microbe_ details what could be a new species and a new genus of such bacteria.

**Read more: “**[**What Do You Know About the Deep-Sea Barbie Pig?**](https://nautil.us/what-do-you-know-about-the-deep-sea-barbie-pig-1285329)**”**

The microbes were found in eight sea pigs collected off the northern coast of Japan in the Northwest Pacific, and they dominated the body walls of the echinoderms—76.4 to 98.9 percent of the bacterial DNA found under the skin was this new species.

“Taxonomic and genomic information about these body-wall inhabiting bacteria is scarce, and very few studies of deep-sea species have linked this information to the bacteria’s location within host tissues,” study author Yu Yoshida explained in a [statement](https://www.u-tokyo.ac.jp/focus/en/press/z0508_00486.html).

Sea pigs are part of the sea cucumber family. _Credit: Nicola Burghall_

Not only is the bacteria new, it’s rather strange as well. It has a stripped-down genome (set of DNA instructions), and yet, it’s still capable of producing giant proteins to carry out work inside cells. The biggest protein the researchers found was 5,475 amino acids long, compared to around 300 for an average bacterial protein.

The study team has suggested _Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola_ for the name of the new species, which roughly translates as the “abyss-dweller that lives in _Scotoplanes_” (_Scotoplanes_ being the genus of the sea pig).

So what does this mean for the jelly-like sea pigs, which waddle along at the bottom of the ocean, picking up dead bits of matter with their tubular feet? Well, we’re not sure. The assumption is they have some kind of mutually beneficial relationship that’s not yet obvious to us.

This much we do know, though: For the inhabitants of the deep ocean, sea pigs are a vital part of the ecosystem. They recycle nutrients and protect other marine life against predators, which is why scientists are keen to learn more about how they thrive and how they’ve evolved.

“We’d really like to understand how this bacterium could become so dominant in the body wall, the functions of the giant surface proteins, what competition it faces from other bacteria, and the effects on the host,” added Yoshida.

Of course, another literal deep dive will be needed to find out more. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: New “Central Dogma of Aging” Highlights the Complexity of Getting Older
content:
Originally proposed by Francis Crick (of Watson and Crick) in 1958, the central dogma of molecular biology states that information flows from DNA to RNA to protein. Now, in a new study [published](https://www.the-innovation.org/article/doi/10.59717/j.xinn-life.2026.100262) in _Innovation Life_, experts on aging have proposed a new central dogma of aging.

For fans of the original central dogma, this new framework has plenty to love. It builds on the trusty DNA → RNA → protein scaffold and adds a fourth layer: metabolites. These small molecules are the end products and intermediaries of the cellular processes that keep you alive, like glucose, ATP, pyruvic acid, and many, many, many more. All four are governed by three processes: anabolism (building up), modification, and catabolism (breaking down).

**Read more: “**[**Can GLP-1s Slow Aging?**](https://nautil.us/can-glp-1s-slow-aging-1285741)**”**

Unlike the traditional central dogma, information within this model flows in multiple directions and problems in one layer can affect the others. As we get older, this interdependent network deteriorates. Take damaged DNA, for example. Faulty genetic material can lead to RNA transcriptional errors, activate inflammation pathways, lead to faulty proteins that occupy cellular recycling processes and throw a wrench into metabolism, etc. Metabolites can then feedback on genetic control via epigenetics. When the four-layer system slips out of balance over time, problems stack up.

Of course, no one ages in a vacuum. So surrounding the four layers is the exposome—the environmental factors that influence the system. These factors can be anything from oxygen and hormones on a micro level to diet, sleep, and pollution on a macro level.

You may be curious why we don’t already have a model for understanding aging, and the truth is we do. The [Hallmarks of Aging](https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(13)00645-4) catalogs a dozen changes that occur in our bodies as we age, like stem cell exhaustion, poorer nutrient sensing, mitochondrial dysfunction, and more.

So why do we need a new one?

According to the team, this new framework offers a more comprehensive understanding of aging and “a novel lens” for “combating aging and age-related decline,” as they write. The researchers characterize the Hallmarks as a kind of parallel checklist that focuses more on DNA changes, largely omitting metabolites and RNA. Under this new model, aging is a complex series of conversations between every part of our cellular machinery.

While it’s still largely hypothetical, it could help explain why single-target aging interventions continue to miss the mark. The bottom line is: Our bodies are complicated machines, aging is a complicated process, and a holistic approach may be our best bet for understanding how to stay healthy into our golden years. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Derelict Soviet Spacecraft? Dark Comet? What the Heck is 1998 KY26?
content:
Hayabusa-2 is currently careening toward a rendezvous with the unknown. Launched in 2014, the Japanese spacecraft embarked on a mission to retrieve samples from asteroids and return them to Earth. It performed its duties admirably in 2018, spending a year and a half surveying the “rubble pile” asteroid Ryugu before swinging by its home planet to drop off the goods. Inside the sample return canister were traces of organic compounds from the dawn of the solar system.

Now its mission has been extended until at least 2031, when it should reach its next target: the smaller, speedier, more mysterious 1998 KY26. This peculiar celestial object has puzzled astronomers since its discovery nearly 30 years ago. It’s relatively tiny—not much bigger than Hayabusa-2 itself and roughly 1/100th the diameter of Ryugu—and it rotates at a brisk clip of once every 5.35 minutes.

**Read more: “**[**Nine Rebel Astronomy Theories That Went Dark**](https://nautil.us/nine-rebel-astronomy-theories-that-went-dark-544315)**”**

But the weirdest thing about 1998 KY26 is its acceleration. Instead of smoothly zipping around the sun like a normal asteroid it tends to lurch perpendicular to its orbit in unpredictable ways. This odd behavior led Harvard astrophysicist [Avi Loeb](https://nautil.us/if-we-believe-in-dark-matter-why-not-extraterrestrial-life-237641) and colleagues to argue it wasn’t an asteroid at all, but the derelict Soviet space probe Phobos 1 (the paper, published earlier this year, hasn’t been peer reviewed).

Of course, there are other explanations for this kind of activity. For example, it’s possible 1998 KY26 is a “dark comet.” Comets get their magnificent tails from the sun heating icy particles that jet out into space. Dark comets, on the other hand, are asteroids that keep their icy material hidden beneath the surface. They can act like comets, but without the telltale tail.

Unfortunately, a new study [published](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0019103526004276) in the journal _Icarus_ is throwing cold water on the dark asteroid theory—or rather, warm regolith. Per an analysis of 1998 KY26 conducted by aerospace engineers from the Georgia Institute of Technology, the object is much too warm to harbor any ice. “Our temperature model results indicate that the water outgassing rate on 1998 KY26 would be too high to maintain buried ice, refining the understanding of the asteroid’s composition,” the researchers wrote. If 1998 KY26 ever had secret pockets of frozen water, they would have been depleted long ago.

So why is this plucky little asteroid so weird?

We still don’t know for sure, but not knowing is the first step on the path toward knowing. While we speculate back on Earth, mark your calendars for July 2031—that’s when Hayabusa-2 makes contact. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: There’s New Hope for Detecting Alzheimer’s Before Cognitive Deficits Manifest
content:
With no cure for Alzheimer’s on the horizon, and our best treatments only slowing the progression of the disease, there’s been an intense effort to find earlier means of detection. Now, a new study [published](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666956026000759?via%3Dihub) in _Neuroimage Reports_ is offering hope of diagnosis even before cognitive symptoms become noticeable.

A team of biomedical imaging specialists, pathologists, and neuroscientists from Johns Hopkins University studied how the brains of older adults changed over time by analyzing hundreds of MRI scans and PET scans. They relied on longitudinal data from two different studies (the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and the Biomarkers of Cognitive Decline Among Normal Individuals study) that included people from across the Alzheimer’s spectrum, from cognitively healthy to full-blown dementia.

**Read more: “[How the Brain’s Failing Trash Compactor Can Contribute to Alzheimer’s Disease](https://nautil.us/how-the-brains-failing-trash-compactor-can-contribute-to-alzheimers-disease-1286581)”**

Two key brain regions started shrinking earlier and faster than the hippocampus: the entorhinal cortex, which functions as the brain’s interface between the hippocampus and the neocortex, and the amygdala, where emotions are processed. Both of these hippocampus-adjacent regions play a role in memory formation and consolidation. PET scans showed that the atrophy of these two areas was associated with local changes in tau protein, one of two proteins that accumulate in the brains of Alzheimer’s patients.

According to the team, these findings show promise for diagnosing the disease before symptoms manifest. “We’ve found that there are early changes in the brain manifesting the clinical biomarkers of atrophy as much as a decade before there are clinical symptoms,” study author Michael Miller explained in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1151916).

Of course, providing earlier diagnosis means more time to delay the disease, which could translate to more cognitively healthy time with your loved ones. “It’s at least a 5-to-10-year play where your brain is changing,” Miller added. “Imagine if we could start to treat the neurodegenerative changes at the two-, three- or four-year point rather than after 15 years when the changes are manifesting in memory symptoms. That’s the great promise here for your loved ones who are at risk.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: J.R.R. Tolkien on Fairy Tales, Language, the Psychology of Fantasy, and Why There’s No Such Thing as Writing “For Children”
content:
[![Image 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/tolkien_perilousrealm.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Tales-Perilous-Realm-J-R-R-Tolkien/dp/0547154119/?tag=braipick-20)_“I do not believe that I have ever written a children’s book,”_ the great [Maurice Sendak](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/maurice-sendak/) once said [in an interview](https://www.themarginalian.org/2011/12/29/tateshorts-maurice-sendak/). _“I don’t write for children,”_ he [told Colbert](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/05/09/grim-colberty-tales-maurice-sendak/). _“I write — and somebody says, ‘That’s for children!’”_ This sentiment — the idea that designating certain types of literature as “children’s” is a choice entirely arbitrary and entirely made by adults — has since been [eloquently echoed by Neil Gaiman](http://explore.noodle.org/post/64133968491/i-dont-think-there-is-such-a-thing-as-a-bad-book), but isn’t, in fact, a new idea.

On March 8, 1939, **J.R.R. Tolkien** (January 3, 1892–September 2, 1973), celebrated as one of the greatest fantasy writers in history, gave a lecture titled “Fairy Stories,” eventually adapted into an essay retitled “On Fairy-Stories” and included in the appendix to [**_Tales from the Perilous Realm_**](https://www.amazon.com/Tales-Perilous-Realm-J-R-R-Tolkien/dp/0547154119/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](http://www.worldcat.org/title/tales-from-the-perilous-realm/oclc/243480382&referer=brief_results)). At the crux of his argument, which explores the nature of fantasy and the cultural role of fairy tales, is the same profound conviction that there is no such thing as writing “for children.”

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/artofthehobbit1.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2011/11/01/art-of-the-hobbit/)

One of Tolkien’s a href=”https://www.themarginalian.org/2011/11/01/art-of-the-hobbit/”>original illustrations for the first edition of _The Hobbit_, 1936

Tolkien begins at the beginning, by defining what a fairy tale is:

> A “fairy-story” is one which touches on or uses Faerie, whatever its own main purpose may be: satire, adventure, morality, fantasy. Faerie itself may perhaps most nearly be translated by Magic — but it is magic of a peculiar mood and power, at the furthest pole from the vulgar devices of the laborious, scientific, magician. There is one proviso: if there is any satire present in the tale, one thing must not be made fun of, the magic itself. That must in that story be taken seriously, neither laughed at nor explained away.

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/hanschristianandersen_ellenderbeverley.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/11/18/taschen-the-fairy-tales-ofhans-christian-andersen/)

Illustration for Hans Christian Andersen’s ‘The Snow Queen’ by Katharine Beverley and Elizabeth Ellender, 1929. Click image for details.

He then explores the relationship between fairy tales and language, denouncing Max Müller’s view of mythology as a “disease of language”:

> Mythology is not a disease at all, though it may like all human things become diseased. You might as well say that thinking is a disease of the mind. It would be more near the truth to say that languages, especially modern European languages, are a disease of mythology. But Language cannot, all the same, be dismissed. The incarnate mind, the tongue, and the tale are in our world coeval. The human mind, endowed with the powers of generalization and abstraction, sees not only green-grass, discriminating it from other things (and finding it fair to look upon), but sees that it is green as well as being grass. But how powerful, how stimulating to the very faculty that produced it, was the invention of the adjective: no spell or incantation in Faerie is more potent. And that is not surprising: such incantations might indeed be said to be only another view of adjectives, a part of speech in a mythical grammar. The mind that thought of light, heavy, grey, yellow, still, swift, also conceived of magic that would make heavy things light and able to fly, turn grey lead into yellow gold, and the still rock into a swift water. If it could do the one, it could do the other; it inevitably did both. When we can take green from grass, blue from heaven, and red from blood, we have already an enchanter’s power — upon one plane; and the desire to wield that power in the world external to our minds awakes. It does not follow that we shall use that power well upon any plane. We may put a deadly green upon a man’s face and produce a horror; we may make the rare and terrible blue moon to shine; or we may cause woods to spring with silver leaves and rams to wear fleeces of gold, and put hot fire into the belly of the cold worm. But in such “fantasy,” as it is called, new form is made; Faerie begins; Man becomes a sub-creator.

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/hanschristianandersen_mauricesendak.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/11/18/taschen-the-fairy-tales-ofhans-christian-andersen/)

Illustration for Hans Christian Andersen’s ‘The Darning Needle’ by Maurice Sendak, 1959. Click image for details.

Like Sendak and Gaiman, Tolkien insists that fairy tales aren’t inherently “for” children but that we, as adults, simply decide that they are, based on a series of misconceptions about both the nature of this literature and the nature of children:

> It is usually assumed that children are the natural or the specially appropriate audience for fairy-stories. In describing a fairy-story which they think adults might possibly read for their own entertainment, reviewers frequently indulge in such waggeries as: “this book is for children from the ages of six to sixty.” But I have never yet seen the puff of a new motor-model that began thus: “this toy will amuse infants from seventeen to seventy”; though that to my mind would be much more appropriate. Is there any essential connexion between children and fairy-stories? Is there any call for comment, if an adult reads them for himself? Reads them as tales, that is, not studies them as curios. Adults are allowed to collect and study anything, even old theatre programmes or paper bags.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Among those who still have enough wisdom not to think fairy-stories pernicious, the common opinion seems to be that there is a natural connexion between the minds of children and fairy-stories, of the same order as the connexion between children’s bodies and milk. I think this is an error; at best an error of false sentiment, and one that is therefore most often made by those who, for whatever private reason (such as childlessness), tend to think of children as a special kind of creature, almost a different race, rather than as normal, if immature, members of a particular family, and of the human family at large.

[![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/07/provensenfairytales10.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/07/16/provensen-book-of-fairy-tales-1971/)

Illustration for Howard Pyle’s ‘The Swan Maiden’ by Alice and Martin Provensen, 1971. Click image for details.

He argues, instead, that the stereotype of fairy tales being associated with children and native to their world is “an accident of our domestic history”:

> Fairy-stories have in the modern lettered world been relegated to the “nursery,” as shabby or old-fashioned furniture is relegated to the play-room, primarily because the adults do not want it, and do not mind if it is misused. It is not the choice of the children which decides this. Children as a class—except in a common lack of experience they are not one—neither like fairy-stories more, nor understand them better than adults do; and no more than they like many other things. They are young and growing, and normally have keen appetites, so the fairy-stories as a rule go down well enough. But in fact only some children, and some adults, have any special taste for them; and when they have it, it is not exclusive, nor even necessarily dominant. It is a taste, too, that would not appear, I think, very early in childhood without artificial stimulus; it is certainly one that does not decrease but increases with age, if it is innate.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> The nursery and schoolroom are merely given such tastes and glimpses of the adult thing as seem fit for them in adult opinion (often much mistaken). Any one of these things would, if left altogether in the nursery, become gravely impaired. So would a beautiful table, a good picture, or a useful machine (such as a microscope), be defaced or broken, if it were left long unregarded in a schoolroom. Fairy-stories banished in this way, cut off from a full adult art, would in the end be ruined; indeed in so far as they have been so banished, they have been ruined.

Tolkien then moves on to the subject of fantasy, a frequently misunderstood faculty of the imagination.

> The mental power of image-making is one thing, or aspect; and it should appropriately be called Imagination. The perception of the image, the grasp of its implications, and the control, which are necessary to a successful expression, may vary in vividness and strength: but this is a difference of degree in Imagination, not a difference in kind. The achievement of the expression, which gives (or seems to give) “the inner consistency of reality,” is indeed another thing, or aspect, needing another name: Art, the operative link between Imagination and the final result, Sub-creation. For my present purpose I require a word which shall embrace both the Sub- creative Art in itself and a quality of strangeness and wonder in the Expression, derived from the Image: a quality essential to fairy-story. I propose, therefore, to arrogate to myself the powers of Humpty-Dumpty, and to use Fantasy for this purpose: in a sense, that is, which combines with its older and higher use as an equivalent of Imagination the derived notions of “unreality” (that is, of unlikeness to the Primary World), of freedom from the domination of observed “fact,” in short of the fantastic. I am thus not only aware but glad of the etymological and semantic connexions of fantasy with fantastic: with images of things that are not only “not actually present,” but which are indeed not to be found in our primary world at all, or are generally believed not to be found there. But while admitting that, I do not assent to the depreciative tone. That the images are of things not in the primary world (if that indeed is possible) is a virtue, not a vice. Fantasy (in this sense) is, I think, not a lower but a higher form of Art, indeed the most nearly pure form, and so (when achieved) the most potent.

[![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/hanschristianandersen_takeotakei.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/11/18/taschen-the-fairy-tales-ofhans-christian-andersen/)

Illustration for the fairy tales of Hans Christian Andersen by Japanese artist Takeo Takei, 1928. Click image for details.

He goes on to argue that, despite the many misconceptions that envelop it, fantasy is far more challenging an art than nonfiction, for it necessitates the creation of an elaborate, immersive world from scratch, without the crutch of reality:

> Fantasy … is difficult to achieve. Fantasy may be, as I think, not less but more sub-creative; but at any rate it is found in practice that “the inner consistency of reality” is more difficult to produce, the more unlike are the images and the rearrangements of primary material to the actual arrangements of the Primary World. It is easier to produce this kind of “reality” with more “sober” material. Fantasy thus, too often, remains undeveloped; it is and has been used frivolously, or only half-seriously, or merely for decoration: it remains merely “fanciful.” Anyone inheriting the fantastic device of human language can say the green sun. Many can then imagine or picture it. But that is not enough — though it may already be a more potent thing than many a “thumbnail sketch” or “transcript of life” that receives literary praise.
> 
> 
> To make a Secondary World inside which the green sun will be credible, commanding Secondary Belief, will probably require labour and thought, and will certainly demand a special skill, a kind of elvish craft. Few attempt such difficult tasks. But when they are attempted and in any degree accomplished then we have a rare achievement of Art: indeed narrative art, story-making in its primary and most potent mode.

[![Image 7](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/08/nielsen_eastofthesun4.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/08/27/kay-nielsen-east-of-the-sun-and-west-of-the-moon/)

Scandinavian fairy tale illustration by Kay Nielsen, 1914. Click image for details.

Tolkien makes a curious argument about the oil-and-water relationship between fantasy and drama, managing to slip in a subtle dig at none other than The Bard:

> In human art Fantasy is a thing best left to words, to true literature. … It is a misfortune that Drama, an art fundamentally distinct from Literature, should so commonly be considered together with it, or as a branch of it. Among these misfortunes we may reckon the depreciation of Fantasy. For in part at least this depreciation is due to the natural desire of critics to cry up the forms of literature or “imagination” that they themselves, innately or by training, prefer. And criticism in a country that has produced so great a Drama, and possesses the works of William Shakespeare, tends to be far too dramatic. But Drama is naturally hostile to Fantasy. Fantasy, even of the simplest kind, hardly ever succeeds in Drama, when that is presented as it should be, visibly and audibly acted. Fantastic forms are not to be counterfeited. Men dressed up as talking animals may achieve buffoonery or mimicry, but they do not achieve Fantasy. . . .
> 
> 
> In Macbeth, when it is read, I find the witches tolerable: they have a narrative function and some hint of dark significance; though they are vulgarized, poor things of their kind. They are almost intolerable in the play. They would be quite intolerable, if I were not fortified by some memory of them as they are in the story as read. I am told that I should feel differently if I had the mind of the period, with its witch-hunts and witch-trials. But that is to say: if I regarded the witches as possible, indeed likely, in the Primary World; in other words, if they ceased to be “Fantasy.” That argument concedes the point. To be dissolved, or to be degraded, is the likely fate of Fantasy when a dramatist tries to use it, even such a dramatist as Shakespeare. Macbeth is indeed a work by a playwright who ought, at least on this occasion, to have written a story, if he had the skill or patience for that art.

[![Image 8](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/10/cummingsfairytales10.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/10/23/e-e-cummings-fairy-tales-john-eaton-1965/)

Illustration for The Fairy Tales of E. E. Cummings by John Eaton, 1965. Click image for details.

Another misconception Tolkien debunks — speaking to Susan Sontag’s conviction that [polarities only rob life of dimension](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/12/03/susan-sontag-stereotypes-polarities/) — is the notion that the fantastical is somehow diametrically opposed to the rational:

> Fantasy is a natural human activity. It certainly does not destroy or even insult Reason; and it does not either blunt the appetite for, nor obscure the perception of, scientific verity. On the contrary. The keener and the clearer is the reason, the better fantasy will it make. If men were ever in a state in which they did not want to know or could not perceive truth (facts or evidence), then Fantasy would languish until they were cured. If they ever get into that state (it would not seem at all impossible), Fantasy will perish, and become Morbid Delusion.
> 
> 
> For creative Fantasy is founded upon the hard recognition that things are so in the world as it appears under the sun; on a recognition of fact, but not a slavery to it. So upon logic was founded the nonsense that displays itself in the tales and rhymes of Lewis Carroll. If men really could not distinguish between frogs and men, fairy-stories about frog-kings would not have arisen.

Returning to his notion of the Secondary World driven by Secondary Belief, Tolkien contributes to [history’s greatest definitions of art](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/06/22/what-is-art/):

> Art is the human process that produces by the way (it is not its only or ultimate object) Secondary Belief.

[![Image 9](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/07/provensenfairytales4.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/07/16/provensen-book-of-fairy-tales-1971/)

Illustration for Seamus MacManus’s ‘Feather O’ My Wing’ by Alice and Martin Provensen, 1971. Click image for details.

He then adds to [the psychological functions of art](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/10/25/art-as-therapy-alain-de-botton-john-armstrong/) by exploring the psychological functions of fairy tales, chief among which is their capacity for rebooting our [chronically blunted attention](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/10/25/art-as-therapy-alain-de-botton-john-armstrong/):

> Recovery (which includes return and renewal of health) is a re-gaining—regaining of a clear view. I do not say “seeing things as they are” and involve myself with the philosophers, though I might venture to say “seeing things as we are (or were) meant to see them”—as things apart from ourselves. We need, in any case, to clean our windows; so that the things seen clearly may be freed from the drab blur of triteness or familiarity—from possessiveness. Of all faces those of our familiares are the ones both most difficult to play fantastic tricks with, and most difficult really to see with fresh attention, perceiving their likeness and unlikeness: that they are faces, and yet unique faces. This triteness is really the penalty of “appropriation”: the things that are trite, or (in a bad sense) familiar, are the things that we have appropriated, legally or mentally. We say we know them. They have become like the things which once attracted us by their glitter, or their colour, or their shape, and we laid hands on them, and then locked them in our hoard, acquired them, and acquiring ceased to look at them.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Creative fantasy, because it is mainly trying to do something else (make something new), may open your hoard and let all the locked things fly away like cage-birds.

[![Image 10](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/10/cummingsfairytales7.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/10/23/e-e-cummings-fairy-tales-john-eaton-1965/)

Illustration for The Fairy Tales of E. E. Cummings by John Eaton, 1965. Click image for details.

The full fifteen-page essay, as well as the rest of [**_Tales from the Perilous Realm_**](https://www.amazon.com/Tales-Perilous-Realm-J-R-R-Tolkien/dp/0547154119/?tag=braipick-20), is well worth a read. Complement it with [Tolkien’s little-known illustrations](https://www.themarginalian.org/2011/11/01/art-of-the-hobbit/) for the first edition of _The Hobbit_.

title: Atom, Archetype, and the Invention of Synchronicity: How Carl Jung and Wolfgang Pauli Bridged Mind and Matter
content:
[![Image 1: Atom, Archetype, and the Invention of Synchronicity: How Carl Jung and Wolfgang Pauli Bridged Mind and Matter](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/atomandarchetype.gif?fit=300%2C464&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Atom-Archetype-Pauli-Letters-1932-1958/dp/069116147X/?tag=braipick-20)

_“Every true theorist is a kind of tamed metaphysicist,”_ Einstein wrote as he contemplated [the human passion for comprehension](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/12/einstein-passion-for-comprehension/) in the final years of his life. He may well have been thinking about the great Austrian-Swiss theoretical physicist **Wolfgang Pauli** (April 25, 1900–December 15, 1958), who first postulated the neutrino and was awarded the Nobel Prize for his discovery of the Pauli exclusion principle — a monumental leap in our understanding of the structure of matter. Decades earlier, 21-year-old Pauli had published a critique of Einstein’s groundbreaking theory of general relativity. It greatly impressed the elder physicist, who wrote in astonishment:

> No one studying this mature, grandly conceived work could believe that the author is a man of 21. One wonders what to admire most, the psychological understanding for the development of ideas, the sureness of mathematical deduction, the profound physical insight, the capacity for lucid systematic presentation, the complete treatment of the subject matter, or the sureness of critical appraisal.

Indeed, this uncommon fusion of psychological acumen and scientific rigor only intensified as Pauli grew older. Around the time he wrote the paper that spurred Einstein’s praise, Pauli became enchanted with the work of pioneering psychologist [William James](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/william-james/). After a three-decade immersion in it, and several years after he won the Nobel Prize in Physics, Pauli met the great psychiatrist **Carl Jung** (July 26, 1875–June 6, 1961), who in turn was deeply influenced by Einstein’s ideas about space and time.

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/jung_pauli.jpg?resize=680%2C387&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Atom-Archetype-Pauli-Letters-1932-1958/dp/069116147X/?tag=braipick-20)

Jung and Pauli struck an unusual friendship, which lasted a quarter century until Pauli’s death and resulted in the invention of synchronicity — acausally connected events, which the observer experiences as having a meaningful connection on the basis of his or her subjective situation, a meeting point of internal and external reality.

Although rooted in Pauli’s interest in dream analysis, their conversations and correspondence went on to explore fundamental questions regarding the nature of reality through the dual lens of physics and psychology. Each used the tools of his expertise to shift the shoreline between the known and the unknown, and together they found common ground in the analogy between the atom, with its nucleus and orbiting electrons, and the self, with its central conscious ego and its ambient unconscious.

Both men were deeply imprinted by this intellectual cross-pollination. In his posthumously published [final work](https://www.amazon.com/Mysterium-Coniunctionis-Separation-Synthesis-Opposites/dp/0710016433/?tag=braipick-20), Jung would write:

> We do not know whether what we on the empirical plane regard as physical may not, in the Unknown beyond our experience, be identical with what on this side of the border we distinguish from the physical as psychic. Though we know from experience that psychic processes are related to material ones, we are not in a position to say in what this relationship consists or how it is possible at all. Precisely because the psychic and the physical are mutually dependent it has often been conjectured that they may be identical somewhere beyond our present experience, though this certainly does not justify the arbitrary hypothesis of either materialism or spiritualism.

Pauli’s parallel curiosity about mind and matter is perhaps best articulated in by his friend and collaborator Werner Heisenberg — he of [uncertainty principle](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/06/08/lori-henriques-heisenbergs-aha/) fame — who would later [write](https://www.amazon.com/Physics-Philosophy-Revolution-Modern-Science/dp/0061209198/?tag=braipick-20):

> Behind [Pauli’s] outward display of criticism and skepticism lay concealed a deep philosophical interest even in those dark areas of reality of the human mind which elude the grasp of reason. And while the power of fascination emanating from Pauli’s analyses of physical problems was admittedly due in some measure to the detailed and penetrating clarity of his formulations, the rest was derived from a constant contact with the field of creative processes, for which no rational formulation as yet exists.

In their conceptually daring correspondence, collected in [**_Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters, 1932–1958_**](https://www.amazon.com/Atom-Archetype-Pauli-Letters-1932-1958/dp/069116147X/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](http://www.worldcat.org/title/atom-and-archetype-the-paulijung-letters-1932-1958/oclc/905324832&referer=brief_results)), the two delve into these parallels between the physical and psychic dimensions of reality. In one of his early letters, Jung considers the analogy Pauli had proposed between the atomic nucleus and the self. He writes in the autumn of 1935:

> Generally speaking, the unconscious is thought of as psychic matter in an individual. However, the self-representation drawn up by the unconscious of its central structure does not accord with this view, for everything points to the fact that the central structure of the collective unconscious cannot be fixed locally but is an ubiquitous existence identical to itself; it must not be seen in spatial terms and consequently, when projected onto space, is to be found everywhere in that space. I even have the feeling that this peculiarity applies to time as well as space… A biological analogy would be the functional structure of a termite colony, possessing only unconscious performing organs, whereas the center, to which all the functions of the parts are related, is invisible and not empirically demonstrable.
> 
> 
> The radioactive nucleus is an excellent symbol for the source of energy of the collective unconscious, the ultimate external stratum of which appears an individual consciousness. As a symbol, it indicates that consciousness does not grow out of any activity that is inherent to it; rather, it is constantly being produced by an energy that comes from the depths of the unconscious and has thus been depicted in the form of rays since time immemorial.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> The center, or the nucleus, has always been for me a symbol of the totality of the psychic, as the conscious plus the unconscious, the center of which does not coincide with the ego as the center of consciousness, and consequently has always been perceived as being external.

![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/carljung_time.jpg?resize=400%2C527&ssl=1)

Carl Jung on the cover of _TIME_ magazine, February 1955

Over the following few years, their correspondence focuses primarily on dream analysis — which both Jung and Pauli saw as a means of illuminating scientific motifs in Pauli’s work — but again and again they return to the symmetry of mind and matter. In a letter to Jung from the summer of 1937, Pauli jeers at the narrow materialism of his own field and calls for an openness to other forms of knowing:

> Most modern physics also lends itself to the symbolic representation of psychic processes, even down to the last detail. Of course, nothing is further from the thoughts of modern man than the idea of penetrating the secrets of matter in this way … since it seems to him that, relatively speaking, less research has been done on the soul, and it is less familiar than matter.

The following summer, 38-year-old Pauli writes:

> After a careful and critical appraisal of the many experiences and arguments, I have come to accept the existence of deeper spiritual layers that cannot be adequately defined by the conventional concept of time.

In 1947, when Jung decided to found an institute dedicated to this field of research, he asked Pauli — who had received the Nobel Prize a year and a half earlier — to be among its sponsors. The physicist gladly agreed. In a letter to Jung from that December, he noted that the parallels between their interests provide “serious evidence that what is developing is indicative of a close fusion of psychology with the scientific experience of the processes in the material physical world.” He peers into that shared future:

> It is probably a long journey, one we are only just setting out on, and it will especially entail, as a modifying factor, constant criticism of the space-time concept.
> 
> 
> Space and time were virtually turned by Newton into God’s right hand (oddly enough, the position made vacant when he expelled the Son of God from there), and it needed an extraordinary mental effort to bring time and space back down from these Olympian heights. Going hand in hand with this, apparently, is the criticism of the basic idea of classical natural science, according to which it describes objective facts to such an extent that there is absolutely no link between them and the researcher (objectifiability of the phenomena independently of the way in which they are observed.)

Four decades before the revered physicist John Archibald Wheeler (who [coined the term “black hole”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/06/27/mapping-the-heavens-natarajan-black-holes/)) made his influential assertion that [“this is a participatory universe [and] observer-participancy gives rise to information,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/09/02/it-from-bit-wheeler/) Pauli plants the seed of a grand question:

> Modern microphysics turns the observer once again into a little lord of creation in his microcosm, with the ability (at least partially) of freedom of choice and fundamentally uncontrollable effects on that which is being observed. But if these phenomena are dependent on how (with what experimental system) they are observed, then is it not possible that they are _also_ phenomena (extra corpus) that depend on _who_ observes them (i.e., on the nature of the psyche of the observer)? And if natural science, in pursuit of the ideal of determinism since Newton, has finally arrived at the stage of the fundamental “perhaps” of the statistical character of natural laws … then should there not be enough room for all those oddities that ultimately rob the distinction between “physics” and “psyche” of all its meaning…?

If you turn Pauli’s words over in your mind for a few moments, you’d realize just how radical and enormous a proposition this is. Indeed, it was this letter that catalyzed the series of conversations in which Pauli and Jung came up with the concept of synchronicity — the ultimate dependency between the observer and the observed. By the fall of 1948, they were using the term regularly in their correspondence. In a letter from mid-1949, Jung writes to Pauli, enclosing a manuscript of his first paper on the subject:

> Quite a while ago, you encouraged me to write down my thoughts on synchronicity… Nowadays, physicists are the only people who are paying serious attention to such ideas.

A few days later, Pauli echoes this faith in interdisciplinary thinking by sharing with Jung one of his great intellectual influences:

> The idea of _meaningful coincidence_ — i.e., simultaneous events not causally connected — was expressed very clearly by Schopenhauer in his essay “On the Apparent Design in the Fate of the Individual.”
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> This essay of Schopenhauer’s had a lasting and fascinating effect on me and seemed to be pointing the way to a new trend in natural sciences. But whereas [he] wanted at all costs to cling to the rigid determinism along the lines of the classical physics of his day, we have now acknowledged that in the nuclear world, physical events cannot be followed in causal chains through time and space. Thus, the readiness to adopt the idea on which your work is based, that of the “meaning as an ordering factor,” is probably considerably greater among physicists than it was in Schopenhauer’s day.

In a subsequent letter from the autumn of 1950, Pauli — who preferred the term “meaning-correspondence” over “synchronicity” as a way of placing greater emphasis on the meaning of events than on their simultaneity — adds:

> In truth, nature is so fashioned that — analogous to Bohr’s [“Complementarity”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/02/complementarity-frank-wilczek-a-beautiful-question/) in physics — any contradiction between causality and synchronically can never be ascertained…. How do the facts that make up modern quantum physics relate to those other phenomena explained by you with the aid of the new principle of synchronicity? First of all, what is certain is that both types of phenomenon go beyond the framework of “classical” determinism.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> I nevertheless, as a physicist, have the impression that the “statistical correspondence” of quantum physics, seen from the point of view of synchronicity, is a very _weak_ generalization of the old causality… Although microphysics allows for an acausal form of observation, it actually has no use for the concept of “meaning.”

In the letter, Pauli diagrams the concepts discussed:

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/pauli_diagram1.jpg?resize=680%2C458&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Atom-Archetype-Pauli-Letters-1932-1958/dp/069116147X/?tag=braipick-20)

Six days later, Jung picks up the thread and crystallizes the definition of synchronicity:

> Synchronicity could be understood as an _ordering system_ by means of which “similar” things coincide, without there being any apparent cause.

With an eye to Pauli’s diagram, he considers the role of space and time in synchronicity:

> Modern physics, having advanced into another world beyond conceivability, cannot dispense with the concept of a space-time continuum. Insofar as psychology penetrates into the unconscious, it probably has no alternative but to acknowledge the “indistinctness” or the impossibility of distinguishing between time and space, as well as their psychic relativity. The world of classical physics has not ceased to exist, and by the same token, the world of consciousness has not lost its validity against the unconscious… “Causality” is a psychologem (and originally a magic _virtus_) that formulates the connection between events and illustrates them as cause and effect. Another (incommensurable) approach that does the same thing in a different way is synchronicity. Both are identical in the higher sense of the term “connection” or “attachment.” But on the empirical and practical level (i.e., in the real world), they are incommensurable and antithetical, like space and time.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> I would now like to propose that instead of “causality” we have “(relatively) constant connection through effect,” and instead of synchronicity we have (relatively) constant connection through contingency, equivalence, or “meaning.”

He illustrates this proposition with his own variation on Pauli’s diagram:

[![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/jung_diagram1.jpg?resize=680%2C390&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Atom-Archetype-Pauli-Letters-1932-1958/dp/069116147X/?tag=braipick-20)

In a letter sent twelve days later, Pauli responds by introducing the crucial concept of scale into these considerations of synchronicity:

> Synchronicity should be defined in a narrower sense so as to comprise effects that only appear when there is a small number of individual cases but disappear when there is a larger number… In quantum physics, there are not just effects that appear with large numbers instead of with small ones, and not only is the term “meaning” not the right one here (which you have written about at great length) but also the concept of the (psychic or psychoid) archetype cannot be used so lightly in the acausalities of microphysics.

In a letter from October of 1953, more than twenty years into their correspondence and a decade into their shared obsession with synchronicity, Jung writes to Pauli:

> It means a lot to me to see how our points of view are getting closer, for if you feel isolated from your contemporaries when grappling with the unconscious, it is also the same with me, in fact more so, since I am actually standing in the isolated area, striving somehow to bridge the gap that separates me from the others. After all, it is no pleasure for me always to be regarded as esoteric. Oddly enough, the problem is still the same 2,000-year-old one: How does one get from Three to Four?

Jung and Pauli unfurl many more fascinating parallels between psychology and physics in the remainder of [**_Atom and Archetype_**](https://www.amazon.com/Atom-Archetype-Pauli-Letters-1932-1958/dp/069116147X/?tag=braipick-20). Complement it with Jung on [human nature](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/07/26/carl-jung-bbc-face-to-face/), then revisit physicist, novelist, and poet Alan Lightman on [science and transcendence](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/01/15/alan-lightman-accidental-universe-science-spirituality/).
